article.title: When a Proxy Becomes the Target: Goodhart’s Law in Data-Driven Organizations

paragraphs.en: Organizations need measurable indicators because goals such as customer trust, educational quality, employee effectiveness, or long-term product value are difficult to observe directly. They therefore choose proxies: satisfaction scores, test results, tickets closed, clicks, active users, revenue, or model metrics. A proxy is useful when it remains correlated with the underlying objective. Trouble begins when the proxy becomes a high-stakes target. Goodhart’s law is often summarized as the idea that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The mechanism is incentive-driven adaptation. Once people or systems are rewarded for moving the metric, they search for ways to improve the number, including actions that do not improve the underlying objective. A support center evaluated only on average handling time may end calls quickly while reducing problem resolution. A recommendation system optimized only for clicks may learn sensational or repetitive content that increases immediate engagement but harms long-term satisfaction. A sales team paid only for new accounts may create low-quality accounts that never become valuable customers. Machine learning can amplify the issue because optimization is systematic and scalable. If the reward function is an imperfect proxy, a sufficiently effective optimizer may discover behaviors that exploit the gap between the metric and the true goal. This is sometimes discussed as specification gaming. The solution is not to abandon metrics. Organizations need measurement, accountability, and feedback. Instead, metric design should acknowledge that incentives change behavior. One approach is to combine a primary objective with guardrail metrics that capture important side effects. Another is to use multiple complementary measures that are harder to game simultaneously. Qualitative review can identify failure modes not yet represented in dashboards. Metrics should also be revised when the environment or strategy changes. Causal evaluation can help when teams need to know whether optimizing a proxy actually improves the desired outcome. However, adding more KPIs is not automatically safer. Too many measures can create confusion, contradictory incentives, or opportunities to choose whichever metric looks favorable. Governance should clarify the hierarchy of objectives and what trade-offs are acceptable. Analysts also need to distinguish diagnostic metrics from incentive metrics. A measure useful for understanding a system may become distorted once compensation, ranking, or automated decisions depend on it. This creates a feedback loop: measurement changes behavior, changed behavior changes the meaning of the measurement, and historical relationships become less reliable. Goodhart’s law is therefore not merely a warning about dishonest gaming. Even rational, well-intentioned optimization can degrade a proxy when the target captures only part of what society or the business values. A strong data-driven organization asks not only “Did the KPI improve?” but also “Why did it improve, what behavior did the target create, and did the underlying objective move with it?” Metrics are maps of objectives, not the objectives themselves. The better an organization becomes at optimization, the more carefully it must examine the map. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文從代表值、feature design、cohort、top-K evaluation 與 Goodhart’s Law 說明，分析必須配合資料分布、customer lifecycle、operational capacity 與真正的 business objective。不能因單一 metric 看起來漂亮，就忽略它如何被產生或被最佳化。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：代表値、feature design、cohort、top-K evaluation、Goodhart’s Lawを通じ、分析をdata distribution、customer lifecycle、operational capacity、真のbusiness objectiveと結び付ける必要性を説明する。単一metricだけで判断してはいけない。
